transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Could you start by telling me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, I came in because I can't seem to stop launching projects. It's like my brain is on overdrive, you know? I've got work plans, certification schedules, I'm upgrading the entire home network... which, by the way, is a nightmare right now because the routers they sell at big box stores are just garbage. I mean, they throttle your bandwidth without telling you, and I had to spend three hours on a forum last night just figuring out how to flash custom firmware onto this one model I bought. Anyway, I'm also messaging all these old contacts, trying to get things moving. It just gets so intense that I blow past normal limits, and I don't even realize it until my wife or my director at work has to step in and tell me to stop. But honestly, if they just let me finish the network setup, everything would be so much faster.
How long has this current stretch of high energy, racing thoughts, and reduced need for stopping projects been going on continuously—days, or weeks?

Well, it's been going on for a while now. I'd say these stretches where I'm just so driven, barely sleeping, feeling like I can take on the world... it's been about a year and eight months of this. Which is funny, because a year and eight months ago is exactly when I decided to completely overhaul our server racks at the office. I mean, they were an absolute mess. Cables everywhere, zero cable management, it looked like a spaghetti factory exploded in there. I spent an entire weekend just color-coding the Ethernet cables. Blue for the main network, yellow for the IP phones, red for the secure lines... you have to use red for secure lines, it's just standard practice, but the guy before me didn't seem to care. He was always leaving early on Fridays anyway, probably going to that golf course out by the highway. I went there once, the greens were terrible. But yeah, about a year and eight months for this energy thing.
During this past year and eight months, have you had any periods—even just a few days at a time—where your mood or energy dropped and you felt noticeably down, low, or depressed?

Yeah, I do get those. There are these stretches where I just wake up feeling... I don't know, like a completely failed version of myself. Just incredibly heavy and flat. It gets to the point where even answering my wife’s normal, everyday questions feels like way too much to handle. 

Like, she’ll ask me something about the grocery list on that new smart fridge she bought. Which, by the way, I specifically told her not to connect to the Wi-Fi. Those IoT devices have absolutely zero built-in security. It's basically an open backdoor into your entire home network. I was reading this security brief a while back where hackers compromised a casino's entire database through a smart thermometer in their lobby fish tank. A fish tank! Can you believe that? I've been meaning to set up a separate VLAN just for her smart appliances so they don't compromise the main network where I do my server testing, but I just haven't had the time to configure the subnet yet. It's a massive vulnerability just waiting to happen. 

But yeah... what were you asking? Oh, right, the low energy. Yeah, I definitely have those heavy days mixed in there.

During these high-energy stretches, has the elevated mood and reduced need for sleep ever lasted at least 7 days in a row without letting up, or has it ever been severe enough that you needed to be hospitalized?

Yeah, oh yeah, definitely. There are weeks—like, a full seven days or more—where I feel almost electric, just completely unstoppable. I'm running on maybe two hours of sleep, but I don't even feel tired. But the thing is, during those weeks, I get so irritable. Like, a tiny delay or just a simple question from my wife can make me snap. It feels like everyone is intentionally trying to slow me down. 

Which reminds me of this guy at the hardware store last Tuesday. I was trying to explain to him why I needed a specific gauge of CAT6 cable for the new server rack, because the standard stuff they sell just doesn't handle the data throughput I need for my home lab. And he just stood there blinking at me. I mean, how do you work in the electrical aisle and not understand basic signal degradation? It's like talking to a wall. I ended up having to order it online anyway, which delayed my whole weekend schedule. The shipping company they use is terrible, too. The tracking said it was "out for delivery" for three days. Three days! I almost drove down to the distribution center myself to find the truck. 

But anyway, yeah, I've definitely had those high-energy stretches last a full week or more, and I just get so frustrated when people can't keep up. Never been hospitalized for it, though. Just... really, really annoyed at everyone.

Right now, over the past week or so, would you say you're primarily in one of those high-energy, wired stretches, or in one of the low, heavy stretches—or are you noticing both the high energy and the low, heavy feelings happening together at the same time?

Right now? Honestly, I'm not really sure which one it is. It's... it's hard to tell over just the last week. I mean, I don't think I'm totally wired, but I wouldn't say I'm completely flat either. It's just a blur. 

Which is exactly what happens when you spend three days staring at endless lines of code trying to debug a firewall configuration. I mean, the logs were an absolute nightmare. Whoever set up the initial routing protocols—probably the same guy who didn't color-code the cables—must have been copying and pasting from some outdated forum from 2012. You can't just leave open ports like that. It's practically an invitation for a DDoS attack. I had to rewrite the entire access control list from scratch. And my wife kept asking me if I wanted dinner, and I'm like, how can I eat when our network security is basically a sieve? I ended up ordering a pizza, but the delivery guy couldn't find our house because the GPS always routes them to the alley behind the neighbor's garage. I've submitted three separate map corrections to Google, but do they update it? Of course not. 

But yeah, the energy thing... I don't really know where I'm at this week. It's just hard to say.

Right now, in this past week, are you noticing both the racing, high-energy feelings AND the heavy, down feelings happening at the same time on the same days, or does it feel more like you're just not experiencing much of either one lately?

Yeah, I guess it feels more like I'm just not experiencing much of either one lately. There have actually been several calm, or I guess you could call them flat stretches, sometimes lasting a few weeks at a time, where I’m not especially up or depressed at all. 

But the thing is, even during those normal weeks when my mood is totally fine, I still see what's going on with the Microsoft Teams statuses. They’re coded warnings. The little colored dots—they aren't just showing who is busy or away, they're signaling who is actively being monitored in the department. I tried explaining this to my director, because honestly, relying on a cloud-based proprietary software for internal corporate comms is a massive privacy violation waiting to happen. I mean, Microsoft forces these updates overnight, and suddenly the UI is different, but they don't give you the patch notes on what telemetry data they're scraping in the background. It’s ridiculous. We should be using a self-hosted, end-to-end encrypted platform on our own hardware, but management won't listen because of "enterprise licensing agreements." It's all just corporate red tape. 

And even when I'm just sitting there, feeling completely level and fine, I still hear these brief comments when no one else is in the room. Just quick little remarks. Usually it happens when I'm in the server room, which, by the way, has a totally inadequate cooling system. I've told building maintenance three times that the ambient intake is pulling in dust from the drop ceiling and clogging the filters on the main switch, but they just log the ticket and close it without even coming upstairs to look. Typical lazy contractors. 

But yeah, to answer your question, lately it's just been pretty flat mood-wise. Not really racing or heavy, just kind of in the middle.

Thinking about those weeks where your mood was flat and completely normal—not high, not low—did the ideas about the Teams status codes being monitoring signals, or hearing those brief comments when no one was around, continue during that whole stretch, for two weeks or more, even though your mood was fine?

Yeah, exactly. During those stretches—like I said, a few weeks at a time where I'm not feeling high or low, just totally flat and normal—I still see the Teams codes. They don't stop just because my mood is stable. And I still hear those little comments, too, even when I'm just sitting there feeling fine. 

Which honestly just proves my point that it's an external monitoring issue and not just me being stressed. I mean, if it was just stress, it would go away when I'm relaxed, right? But the surveillance is constant. It's like how the HR department rolled out that new "wellness tracking" app last month. They claimed it was voluntary, but I analyzed the network traffic on my phone and it was pinging their servers every fifteen minutes with location data. Why does HR need to know if I'm at the grocery store on a Sunday? I ended up putting my phone in a Faraday bag whenever I leave the house now. It's the only way to be sure. My wife thinks I'm being paranoid, but she doesn't understand data packet sniffing. She just clicks "accept" on every Terms of Service without reading a single line. It's terrifying how much people just give away. 

But yeah, those weeks where my mood is totally normal? The Teams warnings and the voices... they're still there. Definitely for two weeks or more at a time.

Looking back over the full year and eight months, would you say the periods of psychotic experiences—like the Teams codes or the comments you hear—occurring without any mood symptoms make up a small fraction of the total time, or do they actually add up to a large part of the whole illness period?

Honestly, looking back over the whole time—what, a year and eight months now?—the high-energy, pressured phases have definitely taken up more of these past couple years than the down periods or those quieter, flat in-between times. It's mostly been that wired feeling. 

Which reminds me, when I'm wired like that, I can actually get a lot done. I built an entire custom NAS enclosure for my home network during one of those stretches. Used a 3D printer for the drive bays and everything. But the filament I bought online was terrible quality—it kept snapping in the extruder. I spent three hours calibrating the nozzle temperature and adjusting the retraction settings, and even then, the layer adhesion was a joke. You really can't trust those cheap off-brand spools from Amazon. They say it's PLA+, but I'm pretty sure it's just recycled plastic with a bunch of cheap fillers. I left a one-star review, but the seller just offered me a $10 gift card to take it down. Obviously, I refused on principle. You can't just bribe people to hide your inferior manufacturing standards. 

But yeah, to answer your question, the wired, high-energy stretches have definitely been the biggest part of the whole time. The quiet times with just the Teams codes and the voices, without the mood stuff, are a smaller piece of the puzzle overall.

But yeah, those weeks where my mood is totally normal? The Teams warnings and the voices... they're still there. Definitely for two weeks or more at a time.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (Teams code delusions, hearing comments) persist for 2+ weeks during euthymic periods, ruling out F31.5 (psychotic features confined to mood episodes). This supports schizoaffective disorder; given clear manic and depressive episodes, F25.0 (bipolar type) remains most likely, with F25.2 (mixed type) still possible.

doctor.intent: Determine the total lifetime duration of psychotic symptoms relative to mood episodes, to assess whether psychotic symptoms have ever occurred predominantly outside mood episodes for a substantial portion of the overall illness (distinguishing F25.0 from F25.2)
doctor.question: Looking back over the full year and eight months, would you say the periods of psychotic experiences—like the Teams codes or the comments you hear—occurring without any mood symptoms make up a small fraction of the total time, or do they actually add up to a large part of the whole illness period?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, the high-energy, pressured phases have taken up more of these past couple years than the down periods or the quieter in-between times.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the mood episodes (or the periods without them) make up the majority of the total illness duration, which directly corresponds to evaluating if the manic episode is present for the majority of the total duration.

patient.answer:
Honestly, looking back over the whole time—what, a year and eight months now?—the high-energy, pressured phases have definitely taken up more of these past couple years than the down periods or those quieter, flat in-between times. It's mostly been that wired feeling. 

Which reminds me, when I'm wired like that, I can actually get a lot done. I built an entire custom NAS enclosure for my home network during one of those stretches. Used a 3D printer for the drive bays and everything. But the filament I bought online was terrible quality—it kept snapping in the extruder. I spent three hours calibrating the nozzle temperature and adjusting the retraction settings, and even then, the layer adhesion was a joke. You really can't trust those cheap off-brand spools from Amazon. They say it's PLA+, but I'm pretty sure it's just recycled plastic with a bunch of cheap fillers. I left a one-star review, but the seller just offered me a $10 gift card to take it down. Obviously, I refused on principle. You can't just bribe people to hide your inferior manufacturing standards. 

But yeah, to answer your question, the wired, high-energy stretches have definitely been the biggest part of the whole time. The quiet times with just the Teams codes and the voices, without the mood stuff, are a smaller piece of the puzzle overall.

inference.note: Patient confirms psychotic symptoms (Teams code delusions, auditory hallucinations) persist for 2+ weeks even during euthymic/flat periods, satisfying the schizoaffective criterion of psychosis without mood symptoms. However, mood episodes (manic-predominant, with depressive episodes) have occupied the majority of the illness course, meeting the mood-duration criterion for schizoaffective disorder. Since the patient denies simultaneous manic and depressive symptoms (endorsing distinct manic, depressive, and euthymic-with-psychosis periods rather than a mixed state), this favors the bipolar type (F25.0) over the mixed/undifferentiated type (F25.2), which is now ruled out.

opening_question.intent: Establish the primary reason for the visit
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Could you start by telling me what's been bringing you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a ~20-month illness course dominated by manic episodes (≥7 days, decreased need for sleep, elevated/irritable mood, increased goal-directed activity, grandiosity about surveillance/network expertise) interspersed with depressive periods, meeting mood episode criteria for Bipolar I. Concurrently, he describes persistent psychotic symptoms—delusional beliefs that Teams status colors and a wellness app represent active surveillance, and auditory hallucinations of comments when alone—that continue unchanged during mood-stable/euthymic periods lasting 2 or more weeks, confirming psychosis independent of mood disturbance. Because mood episodes have been present for the majority of the total illness duration, and psychotic symptoms occur both during and independent of mood episodes, this pattern fits Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type (F25.0) rather than Bipolar Disorder with psychotic features (which requires psychosis only during mood episodes) or Schizophrenia (which would require mood episodes to be brief relative to total illness duration).
